{ "item": { "id": "5ac66235-69dc-4092-b430-9d68837e0c76", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Pipelines", "short_description": "What a pipeline is in Godzilla: a named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector through transform steps to a destination.", "body": "

Pipelines

A pipeline is the core unit of work in Godzilla: a named, versioned data-processing workflow that moves data from a source connector, through zero or more transform steps, to a destination connector. Every pipeline runs as a sequence of events flowing through that path.

Anatomy of a pipeline

Every pipeline has three parts:

  • Source — the connector that emits events into the pipeline (a database, a queue, an upload, a webhook).
  • Transforms — an ordered list of steps that reshape, filter, or enrich events as they pass through. Transforms are optional; a pipeline with none is a pass-through copy.
  • Destination — the connector that events are written to once transforms complete.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Pipelines are declarative|body_html=

You describe the desired source, transforms, and destination; Godzilla schedules and retries the runs. You never manage worker processes directly.

}}

Pipeline state

A pipeline is always in one of three states:

  • draft — configured but not yet processing events.
  • active — running on its configured schedule or trigger.
  • paused — temporarily stopped; resumes from the last checkpoint.

Versioning

Pipeline configuration is versioned. Publishing a new version does not affect events already in flight on the previous version — in-flight runs finish on the version they started on. This matters most when a pipeline definition is part of a larger migration; see the Migration guide for an example of retiring an old pipeline version safely.

Next steps

Ready to build one? Start with the Building your first pipeline guide, or jump straight to the Pipelines endpoint in the API reference.

content.text: Good! Now I need to create the two recipe pages. Let me create "Backfill historical data":

input.short_description: Load historical data into a new destination to catch up with current event streams.
input.body:
Backfill historical data

When connecting a new destination to an existing data source, you often need to load historical data to catch up with current events. This recipe shows how to backfill a destination safely without duplicating ongoing events.

The challenge

Your source system has accumulated months or years of data. You want to:

  • Load all historical data into a new destination
  • Continue receiving new events without gaps or duplicates
  • Know when the backfill is complete
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Backfill timing|body_html=

The key is to backfill before events reach the new destination in the live pipeline, or to use a separate backfill pipeline with a different destination so live and historical data don't conflict.

}}

Approach: Two pipelines

Run two pipelines in parallel:

  1. Historical backfill — a one-time pipeline that reads all past data from your source (filtered by a date range or cursor position) and writes it to the destination.
  2. Live pipeline — your normal, ongoing pipeline that picks up from where backfill stops and continues in real time.

Setting up the backfill pipeline

Create a new pipeline with the same source and destination connectors, but add a source filter to limit events to your historical window:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=backfill-pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={ "name": "backfill-orders-2024", "source": { "connector": "postgres-prod", "query": "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at < '2024-06-01'" }, "destination": "analytics-warehouse" }}}

Once the backfill completes, your live pipeline can start fresh (or resume from the backfill checkpoint) and add only new events.

Monitoring and handoff

  • Check the Run Details page to see when the backfill finishes.

input.short_description: Load historical data into a new destination to catch up with current event streams.
input.body:
Backfill historical data

When connecting a new destination to an existing data source, you often need to load historical data to catch up with current events. This recipe shows how to backfill a destination safely without duplicating ongoing events.

The challenge

Your source system has accumulated months or years of data. You want to:

  • Load all historical data into a new destination
  • Continue receiving new events without gaps or duplicates
  • Know when the backfill is complete
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Backfill timing|body_html=

The key is to backfill before events reach the new destination in the live pipeline, or to use a separate backfill pipeline with a different destination so live and historical data don't conflict.

}}

Approach: Two pipelines

Run two pipelines in parallel:

  1. Historical backfill — a one-time pipeline that reads all past data from your source (filtered by a date range or cursor position) and writes it to the destination.
  2. Live pipeline — your normal, ongoing pipeline that picks up from where backfill stops and continues in real time.

Setting up the backfill pipeline

Create a new pipeline with the same source and destination connectors, but add a source filter to limit events to your historical window:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=backfill-pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={ "name": "backfill-orders-2024", "source": { "connector": "postgres-prod", "query": "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at < '2024-06-01'" }, "destination": "analytics-warehouse" }}}

Once the backfill completes, your live pipeline can start fresh (or resume from the backfill checkpoint) and add only new events.

Monitoring and handoff

  • Check the Run Details page to see when the backfill finishes.
  • Verify row counts in your destination to confirm all historical data arrived.
  • Start or resume your live pipeline once backfill is complete.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Watch for timeouts|body_html=

Very large backfills (millions of rows) may take hours. Use a destination that supports bulk loading, and consider breaking the backfill into smaller date windows if the pipeline times out.

}}

Next steps

See Building your first pipeline for the full step-by-step guide to creating pipelines.

input.short_description: Send the same events to multiple destinations with a single pipeline.
input.body:
Fan-out to multiple destinations

Often you need to send the same events to multiple systems: a data warehouse for analytics, a cache for real-time lookups, and a notification service for alerts. Rather than run separate pipelines for each destination, you can use a single fan-out pattern to send events to all of them.

The challenge

You have a source of events (orders, user signups, sensor readings) that need to arrive at multiple consumers. You want to:

  • Process events once from the source
  • Deliver them reliably to each destination
  • Avoid duplicates and ensure ordering
  • Monitor each destination separately

Approach: Fan-out with transforms

Create a single pipeline that receives events from your source, applies any shared transforms, then delivers them to each destination via a fan-out step:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=fanout-pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={ "name": "user-events-fanout", "source": "kafka-prod", "transforms": [ { "type": "fan_out", "targets": [ { "destination": "analytics-warehouse", "transform": "SELECT * FROM $input" }, { "destination": "redis-cache", "transform": "SELECT user_id, email, status FROM $input" }, { "destination": "slack-alerts", "transform": "SELECT user_id, event_type FROM $input WHERE event_type IN ('critical', 'alert')" } ] } ] }}}

Key benefits

  • Single source of truth — one pipeline definition, one failure point to monitor.
  • Efficient — events are read from the source once and fanned out to all destinations.
  • Flexible transforms — each destination can receive a different subset or shape of the event.
  • Ordered delivery — events reach all destinations in the same order they were emitted.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Per-destination retries|body_html=

If one destination fails, Godzilla retries it independently; other destinations continue receiving events. Use dead-letter queues to capture failures per destination.

}}

Monitoring fan-out pipelines

In the Run Details page, you'll see:

  • Total events ingested — how many events the source emitted
  • Per-destination delivery — success/failure counts for each target
  • Latency breakdown — time to fan-out vs. time to each destination

Set up alerts on any destination that starts failing, so you catch issues before data gaps appear.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Fan-out limits|body_html=

Most sources can fan out to 3–5 destinations efficiently. Beyond that, consider running a dedicated aggregation pipeline or splitting into multiple fan-out pipelines by event type.

}}

Next steps

See Building your first pipeline to learn pipeline basics, or explore Monitoring & alerts for production-ready observability.
